'''yarwhip''' (yär′hwip), ''n.'' Same as ''yarwhelp''.

'''yashmak''' (yash′mak), ''n.'' [Ar.] The veil worn by Moslem women in public—that is, when not in their own apartments.
{{smaller block|The ''yashmak'' is a sort of double veil. The first brought round the forehead and gathered neatly up behind and on the head; the second, pinned on behind to the first, falls sufficiently in front to uncover the eyes.
{{right|''E. Sartorius'', In the Soudan, p. 19.}}}}

Wi’ winged spurs did ride.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', Election Ballads, iv.}}}}
{{smaller block|I will content me with . . . the haunch and the nombles [of venison], and e’en heave up the rest on the old oak-tree yonder, and come back for it with one of the ''yauds''.
{{right|''Scott'', Monastery, xvii.}}}}

'''yaul''', ''n.'' See ''yawl''<sup>2</sup>.

{{smaller block|A very red-faced, thick-lipped countryman, . . . as soon as the Prince hailed him, jovially, if somewhat thickly, answered. At the same time he gave a beery ''yaw'' in the saddle.
{{right|''R. L. Stevenson'', Prince Otto, i. 4.}}}}

'''yaw<sup>2</sup>''' (yâ), ''n.'' [Said to be from African ''yaw'', a raspberry.] '''1.''' One of the tubercles characteristic of the disease known as yaws.
{{smaller block|In some cases a few ''yaws'' will show themselves long after the primary attack is over; these are called “memba ''yaws''” (from “remember”).
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XXIV. 732.}}}}
'''2.''' A thin or defective place in cloth.

'''yaw<sup>2</sup>''' (yâ), ''v. i.'' [< ''yaw''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.''] To rise in blisters, breaking in white froth, as cane-juice in the sugar-works.

'''yawd''' (yâd), ''n.'' A Scotch form of ''jade''<sup>1</sup>.

'''yawey''' (yâ′i), ''a.'' [< ''yaw''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ey''.] Pertaining to or characteristic of the yaws.
{{smaller block|That yaws is a communicable disease is beyond question; but that it has always arisen by conveyance of ''yawey'' matter from a previous case is neither proved nor probable.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XXIV. 732.}}}}

'''yawl<sup>1</sup>''' (yâl), ''v. i.'' [Also ''yowl''; formerly also ''yole'' and ''gowl''; < ME. ''goulen'', < Icel. ''gaula'' = LG. ''gaueln'' = G. ''jaulen'', howl, yell; an imitative word, like ''howl''; it may be regarded as a more sonorous form of ''yell''<sup>1</sup>.] To cry out; howl; yell.
{{smaller block|<poem>He hurtez of the houndez, & thay
Ful ȝomerly ''ȝaule'' & ȝelle.</poem>
{{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1451.}}
<poem>My little legs still crossing
His: either kicking this way, that way sprawling,
Or, if hee but remov’d me, straitwaies ''yawling.''</poem>
{{right|''Heywood'', Dialogues (Works, ed. Pearson, 1874, VI. 201).}}
<poem>Then yelp’d the cur, and ''yawl’d'' the cat.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', The Goose.}}}}

'''yawl<sup>2</sup>''' (yâl), ''n.'' [Sometimes also ''yaul''; < MD. *''jolle'' (in dim. ''jolleken''), D. ''jol'', a yawl, skiff, = Dan. ''jolle'' = Sw. ''julle'', a yawl, jolly-boat. Cf. ''jolly-boat.''] '''1.''' A ship’s small boat, usually rowed by four or six oars; a jolly-boat.—'''2.''' The smallest boat used by fishermen. See cut under ''rowlock.''—'''3.''' A sail-boat or small yacht of the cutter class, with a jigger and short main-boom.

'''yawn''' (yân), ''v.'' [Early mod. E. ''yane'', dial. ''gaun'', ''goan''; < ME. ''ȝanon'', ''ȝonen'', ''ganen'', ''gonen'', < AS. ''gānian'' = LG. ''janen'' = OHG. ''geinōn'', MHG. ''geinen'', yawn; a secondary form, parallel to AS. ''ginian'' = OHG. ''ginēn'', MHG. ''ginen'', ''genen'', G. ''gähnen'', yawn; both being derived from a strong verb, AS. ''gīnan'' (pret. *''gān''), in comp. ''tō-gīnen'', gape apart, = Icel. ''gīna'', gape: see further under ''begin.'' The form ''yawn'', < AS. ''gānian'', instead of *''yone'' (yōn), is irreg., but is parallel with ''broad'' (brôd), < AS. ''brād.'' The initial ''y'' for ''g'' is also irregular; it is prob. due to an AS. var. *''geánian'', or to conformation with ''yave'' for ''gave'', etc.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To gape; open; stand wide.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then from the ''yawning'' wound with fury tore
The spear, pursu’d by gushing streams of gore.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xii. 479.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Crowds that stream from ''yawning'' doors.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, lxx.}}}}
readings.c3s2:
'''2.''' To express or utter with a yawn.
{{smaller block|<poem>“Heigho,” ''yawned'' one day King Francis,
“Distance all value enhances!”</poem>
{{right|''Browning'', The Glove.}}}}

'''yawn''' (yân), ''n.'' [< ''yawn'', ''v.''] '''1.''' The act of gaping or opening wide.
{{smaller block|<poem>Sometimes with a mighty ''yawn'', ’tis said,
Opens a dismal passage to the dead.</poem>
{{right|''Addison'', tr. from Silius Italicus’s Punicorum, ii.}}}}
'''2.''' An involuntary opening of the mouth from drowsiness; oscitation. See ''yawning''.
{{smaller block|<poem>From every side they hurried in,
Rubbing their sleepy eyes with lazy wrists,
And doubling overhead their little fists
In backward ''yawns''.</poem>
{{right|''Keats'', Endymion, ii.}}
The family is astir; and member after member appears with the morning ''yawn''.
{{right|''C. D. Warner'', Backlog Studies, p. 20.}}}}
'''3.''' An opening; a chasm. ''Marston''.
{{smaller block|<poem>But June is full of invitations sweet,
Forth from the chimney’s ''yawn'' and thrice-read tomes.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Under the Willows.}}
Through the ''yawns'' of the back-door, and sundry rents in the logs of the house, filter in, unweariedly, fine particles of snow.
{{right|''S. Judd'', Margaret, i. 17.}}}}
readings.c3s3:
¶
'''yawner''' (yâ′nėr), ''n.'' One who yawns.

'''yawning''' (yâ′ning), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''yawn'', ''v.''] Gaping; oscitation; the taking of a deep inspiration, followed by a slight pause, and then a prolonged expiration, the mouth being more or less widely open. {{smaller|The act is reflex and involuntary in character, though it can often be partially repressed by a strong effort of the will. It is the physiological expression of fatigue and of a desire to sleep, but is also excited by insufficient oxygenation of the blood, and occurs therefore in conditions of lowered vitality, in the prodromal stage of many diseases, and after profuse losses of blood. The sight of another person yawning is also provocative of the act.}}

'''yawningly''' (yâ′ning-li), ''adv.'' In a yawning manner; with yawns or gapes.
{{smaller block|Ye . . . that leaning upon your idle elbow ''yawningly'' patter out those prayers.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', The Hypocrite, Sermon on 2 Tim. iii. 5.}}
Many were merely attracted by a new face, and, having stared me full in the title-page, walked off without saying a word; while others lingered ''yawningly'' through the preface, and, having gratified their short-lived curiosity, soon dropped off one by one.
{{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 358.}}}}

'''yawp''' (yâp), ''v.'' and ''n.'' A dialectal form of ''yelp''.

'''yaws''' (yâz), ''n. pl.'' [Pl. of ''yaw''<sup>2</sup>.] A contagious disease of the skin, endemic in many tropical regions: same as ''frambœsia''.

'''yaw-weed''' (yâ′wēd), ''n.'' A shrubby West Indian plant, ''Morinda Royoc'', used as a remedy for the yaws or frambœsia.

'''Yb.''' In ''chem.'', the symbol for ''ytterbium''.

'''Y. B.''' An abbreviation of ''year-book''.

'''Y-branch''' (wī′branch), ''n.'' See ''branch'', 2 (''e'').

'''Y-cartilage''' (wī′kär″ti-lạ̄j), ''n.'' The ypsiliform cartilage uniting the ilium, ischium, and pubis at the acetabulum, ossified about the age of puberty.

'''ychone†, ychoone†.''' Middle English forms of ''each one.''
{{smaller block|With myrthe and with mynstrasye thei pleseden hir ''ychoone.''
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (A), iii. 98.}}}}

{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, v. 2. 120.}}}}
{{smaller block|She steered wild, ''yawed'', and decreased in her rate of sailing. ''Marryat'', Frank Mildmay, xx. (''Davies.'')

The language [German] has such a fatal genius for going stern foremost, for ''yawing'', and for not minding the helm without some ten minutes’ notice in advance, that he must be a great sailor indeed who can safely make it the vehicle for anything but imperishable commodities.
{{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 1st ser., p. 293.}}}}
{{smaller block|The sun flashed on her streaming ebony black sides as she ''yawed'' to the great ocean swell that chased her.
{{right|''W. C. Russell'', Sailor’s Sweetheart, v.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To move aside; move from one side to the other. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>My eyes! how she [a mare] did pitch! . . .
And ''yaw’d'' her head about all sorts of ways.</poem>
{{right|''Hood'', Sailor’s Apology for Bow-legs.}}}}

'''yaw<sup>1</sup>''' (yâ), ''n.''   [< ''yaw''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   ''Naut.'', a temporary deviation of a ship or vessel from the direct line of her course.
{{smaller block|<poem>O, the ''yaws'' that she will make!</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher and Massinger'', A Very Woman, iii. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|He did not see a light just before us, which had been hid by the studding-sails from the man at the helm, but by an accidental ''yaw'' of the ship was discovered.

{{smaller block|<poem>Then from the ''yawning'' wound with fury tore

{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xii. 479.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Crowds that stream from ''yawning'' doors.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, lxx.}}}}

{{smaller block|The cracks and rents that had fissured their [the kilns’] walls, from the fierce heat that once blazed within, were ''yawning'' hideously.|{{right|''Geikie'', Geol. Sketches, i.}}}}
Specifically — '''2.''' To open the mouth wide. (''a'') Voluntarily.
{{smaller block|The crocodiles not only know the voice of the priests when they call unto them, and endure to be handled and stroked by them, but also ''yawn'' and offer their teeth unto them to be picked and cleansed with their hands.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 794.}}}}
(''b'') Involuntarily, as through drowsiness or dullness; gape; oscitate. Compare ''yawning''.
{{smaller block|When a man ''yawneth'' he cannot hear so well.
{{right|''Bacon'', Nat. Hist., § 283.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>At every line they stretch, they ''yawn'', they doze.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Dunciad, ii. 390.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And, leaning back, he ''yawned'' and fell asleep,
Lulled by the chant monotonous and deep.</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', Wayside Inn, The Sicilian’s Tale.}}}}
'''3.''' To gape, as in hunger or thirst for something; hence, to be eager; long.
{{smaller block|The chiefest thing which lay-reformers ''yawn'' for is that the clergy may through conformity in state and condition be apostolical, poor as the Apostles of Christ were poor.
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, Pref., iv. § 3.}}}}
'''4.''' To be open-mouthed with surprise, bewilderment, etc.; be agape.
{{smaller block|<poem>To ''yawn'', be still, and wonder,
When one but of my ordinance stood up
To speak of peace or war. ''Shak.'', Cor., iii. 2. 11.</poem>}}

A horrid Thunder in her bowels rumbles, . . .
Tearing her Rocks, Vntill she ''Yawn'' a way
To let it out, and to let-in the Day.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Lawe.}}}} '''2.''' To express or utter with a yawn.

'''yawp''' (yâp), ''v.'' and ''n.'' A dialectal form of ''yelp''.

'''yaws''' (yâz), ''n. pl.''   [Pl. of ''yaw''<sup>2</sup>.]   A contagious disease of the skin, endemic in many tropical regions: same as ''frambœsia''.

'''yaw-weed''' (yâ′wēd), ''n.'' A shrubby West Indian plant, ''Morinda Royoc'', used as a remedy for the yaws or frambœsia.

'''Yb.''' In ''chem.'', the symbol for ''ytterbium''.

'''Y. B.''' An abbreviation of ''year-book''.

'''Y-branch''' (wī′branch), ''n.'' See ''branch'', 2 (''e'').

'''Y-cartilage''' (wī′kär″ti-lạ̄j), ''n.'' The ypsiliform cartilage uniting the ilium, ischium, and pubis at the acetabulum, ossified about the age of puberty.

'''ychone†, ychoone†.''' Middle English forms of ''each one.''
